summary: The note surveys the rise of urban reforestation initiatives in cities worldwide since September 2023. It covers green infrastructure, community campaigns, wildlife corridors, school programs, municipal policy, smart technology, corporate programs and climate resilience. It argues that tree planting is part of a broader approach to urban sustainability.
one_line: Overview of urban reforestation initiatives since September 2023, spanning community, policy, technology, corporate and climate resilience efforts in cities.
key_facts: Since September 2023 there has been a notable increase in the number of urban reforestation projects.
Maria Gonzalez, an urban ecologist, and Jaime Lerner, a former city planner known for revitalizing Curitiba, are named as pioneers of urban forestry efforts.
Green infrastructure includes green roofs and walls, urban gardens, and native flora in public parks and along city streets.
The "Each One, Plant One" campaign launched in New York City on December 10th, 2023, encouraging each resident to plant at least one tree.
The Liberty Wildlife Corridor in Philadelphia was inaugurated on April 22nd, 2024, as a habitat for both people and wildlife.

School programs introduced since fall 2023 have raised environmental literacy; biophilic classroom designs with live plants and natural light are linked to improved student concentration and well-being.

San Francisco's Urban Forest Plan, spearheaded by Mayor Thomas O’Connor, was established on January 15th, 2024, and supports tree planting and maintenance through funding and clear planting guidelines.
Smart sensors and satellite imagery are used to monitor tree health, optimize water usage and detect disease.
Dr. Ian Smith and his team have worked on drone-planting technology since September 2023.
Fashion company Verve launched the Green Steps program on October 21st, 2023, committing to plant a tree for every item sold, resulting in thousands of urban trees.
Trees provide shade that lowers urban temperatures, reducing the heat island effect.
Trees absorb stormwater runoff, minimizing flooding risks and easing the burden on city drainage systems.
